claims.text: The as-deposited multilayer high-entropy-alloy coatings have well-defined, coherent interfaces between layers.
Coherent multilayer interfaces act as barriers that pin dislocations.
Dislocations nucleate during deformation of the coatings.
Dislocations accumulate at multilayer interfaces when their motion is impeded.
Interfacial pinning forces dislocations to move through climb and cross-slip.
Dislocation climb and cross-slip are higher-energy processes than unobstructed dislocation motion.
Forcing dislocations into climb and cross-slip reduces the time-dependent plastic-strain rate.
Dislocation climb is active over the proposed room-temperature-to-moderately-elevated-temperature test range.
The coatings should be subjected to sustained constant-load creep or nanoindentation tests at controlled temperatures.
Multilayer and monolithic coatings should be tested under identical load and temperature conditions.
Multilayer coatings should have a significantly lower steady-state creep-strain rate than equivalent monolithic coatings.
Multilayer coatings should exhibit delayed plastic deformation relative to monolithic coatings.
The enhanced creep resistance applies while the multilayer interfaces remain stable.
Very high temperatures can degrade multilayer interfaces through diffusion or coarsening.
Interfacial degradation diminishes the proposed resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
The contribution of interface strength and interface density to creep resistance may depend on alloy composition and processing history.
In situ microscopy, nanoindentation, and electron microscopy will be used to measure strain evolution, dislocation pile-up, and interface integrity.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or interfacial dislocation accumulation in the multilayer coating would falsify the hypothesis.
